subject: Modeling help - estimating relative likelihood of different time series models

messages.author: e1c430550f86b1f6
messages.subject: Modeling help - estimating relative likelihood of different time series models
parts:
Hi all,

I have a set of time series values (positive) of y:

vector<lower=0>[N] y

I want to estimate the relative likelihood of the following 3 scenarios:

a. diverging AR(1):     y_n ~ normal (alpha + y_(n-1), sigma), alpha > 0
b. converging AR(1):  y_n ~ normal (alpha + y_(n-1), sigma), alpha < 0
c. stationary:             y_n ~ normal (mu, sigma)

What would be the best way to do this in STAN?

Many thanks,
Andy

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Modeling help - estimating relative likelihood of different time series models
parts:
To discriminate between (a) and (b) you can just
run a model with alpha unconstrained and consider

p(alpha > 0) = n(alpha > 0) / n.

The alpha=0 case is tricker because it has zero
measure compared to the others and you need
to do proper model comparison.  Cross validation,
as approximated by the loo package, would be
one such approach.

messages.author: 37f85c6188fe5eeb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Modeling help - estimating relative likelihood of different time series models
parts:
You might think about defining what it means for alpha to have no practical significance for your timeseries. Like for example if abs(alpha) < SomeValue

For example if you are observing for a year and the cumulative effect of alpha over a year is less than the measurement error in one observation, or something like that.

Also, I think there's something amiss with your model. y is positive, but if y_0 is small enough and alpha is negative, then the average value of the next step is negative!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Modeling help - estimating relative likelihood of different time series models
parts:
hmm, maybe I'm missing something but don't you need an autoregressive parameter beta, e.g.:

y_n ~ normal (alpha + beta * y_(n-1), sigma)

In which case, couldn't you just fit one model, and see whether alpha > 0 or < 0 and whether beta is "significant"?

Seth
